=== PEDAGOGY DOCUMENT ===
National Curriculum Framework for School Education
4.4.2.2 Secondary Stage — Science Pedagogy Context
4.6.1 Pedagogy for Science


4.6.1 Pedagogy for Science

Learning Science involves not just learning theories and facts of Science, but also making
connections between conceptual learning and real life, acquiring the capacities of scientific
inquiry, and most importantly, applying these to understanding the world.

Students like to explore the world around them and understand why and how things happen. In
this process of exploration, they use trial-and-error methods to test their hypotheses and reach
possible conclusions. This exploration need not take place individually — students learn Science
best through engaging with peers and adults.

Students have theories about why things happen, patterns they see around them, and about
cause-and-effect relationships. As they learn about Science in a more formal set-up, these ideas
get tested. Some concepts fit into the students' current understanding, while others require a
shift in thinking. If there is an alignment between current ideas and what is discussed in
classrooms, ideas get strengthened.

At the same time, some concepts do not fit into the students' current thinking. If not addressed,
they can turn into alternative conceptions. For example, heavy objects fall faster, plants are non-
living because they don't move, or heavy/big objects always sink in water. If these ideas are not
challenged and suitably modified through investigation, they can turn into alternative conceptions
which may persist as students move through school.

Apart from these theories, students also bring with them the ability to reason, understand, and
explain relationships between cause and effect. These capacities serve as the basis for developing
scientific reasoning. Opportunities, therefore, to inquire are important, as opposed to being 'told'.
Scientific values, such as honesty and integrity, also develop through 'doing Science'. For example,
while demonstrating an experiment on the boiling point of water, we should write the reading on
the thermometer accurately, even if the water is not boiling at 100 degrees.

The role of the Teacher in aligning pedagogy and assessment with how students learn Science is
critical. Teachers must build an environment that promotes natural curiosity, encourages
questions, gives maximum possible opportunities for hands-on activities, and gives ample space
to discuss ideas. Opportunities for students to express their understanding through different
modes and formative assessments to track growing understanding are also key to learning
Science.

4.6.1.1 Pedagogic Principles

Science pedagogy across stages must be informed by the following principles:

a. Learning Science requires an active engagement of students with the world around them to
   understand it. Science pedagogy achieves this through:
   i.  Simulating the processes of Science such as asking questions, hypothesising, observing,
       testing, finding evidence, collecting data, analysing, modifying conclusions,
       communicating, and re-questioning.
   ii. Exposing students to a variety of aspects of learning Science in varied settings — the
       laboratory, classroom, and field — through approaches such as inquiry, discovery,
       didactic, hands-on Science.
   iii. Encouraging and sustaining curiosity by providing varied experiences that may
        challenge students' existing notions and ideas.

b. Learning Science requires communication and sharing of ideas and observations. Science
   pedagogy achieves this through:
   i.  Using scientific vocabulary during instruction and creating a variety of contexts and
       situations for students to communicate their understanding, ideas, and observations.
   ii. Peer and collaborative learning.

c. Learning Science requires a gradual increase in the capacity to engage with complex and
   abstract ideas, aligned with the cognitive and procedural capacities of students. Science
   pedagogy achieves this by building on students' existing knowledge and using multiple
   representations (mathematical, graphical, diagrammatic, and models).

d. Learning Science requires making linkages between knowledge for the holistic and
   multidisciplinary learning emphasised in NEP 2020. Science pedagogy achieves this
   through:
   i.  Connecting scientific knowledge inside and outside the classroom.
   ii. Horizontal connections with other curricular areas.

e. Learning Science enables the development of certain values, such as collaboration,
   sensitivity, empathy, equality of opportunities, respect for diversity, and other values
   mentioned in NEP 2020. Science pedagogy must facilitate this process.

4.6.1.2 Recommended Pedagogical Approaches and Settings

The same pedagogical approach can be used across the three settings most suitable for learning
Science — the classroom, the field, and the laboratory. The following is a list of considerations
based on which Teachers can choose pedagogical approaches and settings:

a. The nature of a concept should guide the decision regarding the approach and setting.
   For example, speed can be discussed in the playing field, but the structure of a cell
   requires a microscope.
b. The approach and setting chosen should enable the attainment of learning outcomes
   and competencies.
c. Each of the recommended approaches and settings must be selected at least once in an
   academic year, if not more. This will ensure exposure to varied approaches and settings.
d. Even when Teachers choose a didactic approach, areas that students could have
   potentially inquired about or discovered should be highlighted.

a. Hands-on Science
The most important part of learning Science is actually 'doing Science' through hands-on
experiential learning. 'Doing Science' can range from trial and error, using materials around
them, or using basic scientific instruments (measuring instruments), and laboratory apparatus.
In this process, students gain conceptual understanding and develop capacities through
manipulating, designing, and building experiments and demonstrations.

b. Discovery approach
Students explore the natural world following their own interests and discover patterns of
how the world works during their explorations. Teachers may also create opportunities or
draw attention to natural phenomena that students can explore further. Often, this discovery
is followed by other, more structured approaches to ensure learning. For example, the Teacher
draws the attention of the students to changes in the length of the shadows as the day
progresses or to the venation patterns of the leaves of different plants. Students' observations
on shadows are then connected to scientific concepts such as the path of light, and the
venation pattern is connected to the shapes of the leaves.

c. Inquiry approach
The inquiry approach allows students to navigate through unknown questions and explore
solutions on their own. It allows students to work in the same way as scientists. The inquiry
approach engages students with systematic observation, visualising, experimenting, inferring,
communicating, and discovering relations. This approach allows Teachers to choose the
appropriate type of inquiry with respect to the concept and to scaffold (support as per need)
students' learning. For example, students could explore questions such as: How do the image
characteristics vary with the relative position between lens and object? How does the surface
area of the reactants affect the rate of reaction? How does the intensity of light affect the rate
of photosynthesis?

d. Project-centred approach
This approach allows learning within the classroom to continue outside the classroom and
extend over a period of time. For example, observing the changes in the moon over a month
to understand the phases of the moon. In this process, connections to daily life are also made.
The project-centred approach allows students to develop artefacts/products (charts,
presentations, speeches) that reflect and communicate their emerging understanding. It also
allows the integration of concepts across different curricular areas.

e. Didactic approach
Often, teaching Science involves communicating certain important information in the form of
scientific terms, phenomena, and the historical development of concepts and ideas. In this
approach, the Teacher largely regulates the direction and flow of the lesson.

f. Demonstration
The Teacher demonstrates the working of certain instruments or outcomes of experimental
set-ups to draw the attention of the students to relevant concepts. These demonstrations
enrich students' learning experiences of the concepts.

Teacher's Voice 4.6i — Demonstrating Osmosis in Living Cells (Grade 9)
For my Grade 9 students, I planned a demonstration of osmosis in living cells. They already
are familiar with the concept in form of daily life examples such as what causes pruning of
our fingers if kept in water for long, but in this session, we go a level deeper to observe the
process in living cells under the microscope.

We will have a total of 90 minutes to perform this. Hence, I prepare the material such as
common salt (NaCl) solution and cut onion pieces and equipment such as glass slides,
forceps, and microscopes. Students work in multiple groups. Hence, I prepare as many
instruction/observation recording sheets.

On that day, I begin by demonstrating the experiment — I prepare three slides A, B and C,
add drops of solution in varying quantity, place coverslip, and then observe under the
microscope what is happening to the cells in the onion peel on the slide.

Then all groups repeat this same set of actions and record their observation by drawing
on the sheet provided. Post this, we discuss whatever we observed. After the students
discuss possible inferences, I introduce the term 'osmosis' to the class, using the concept
to explain their observations and share more daily life examples where we see this
phenomena — for example, in the process of pickling.

=== CHAPTER SUMMARY ===
Chapter 9: Atomic Foundations of Matter

9.1 Law of Conservation of Mass

This section opens by asking whether mass changes during physical and chemical changes, using the example of water whose properties differ entirely from its constituent elements hydrogen and oxygen, yet whose mass equals the sum of their masses. Three numbered activities anchor the section's central claim. Activity 9.1 investigates a physical change: students dissolve common salt in water and find that the mass of the resulting solution equals the sum of the masses of water and salt taken, establishing that mass is conserved in physical changes. (Activity 9.1) Students dissolve a spatula of common salt in about 50 mL of water in a tared beaker and confirm that the reading before and after dissolution does not change.

Activity 9.2 tests whether mass is also conserved in chemical changes by reacting vinegar with baking soda (sodium hydrogencarbonate), which produces carbon dioxide. Two experimental set-ups are used: in set-up 1, the balloon with baking soda sits beside the conical flask and gas escapes after mixing, producing a lower final reading; in set-up 2, the balloon is fixed to the flask mouth so all gases are captured, and the final reading matches the initial reading, confirming mass conservation even in chemical reactions. (Activity 9.2) Students in two set-ups weigh vinegar and baking soda before and after reaction, discovering that only when the system is closed—gas captured in the balloon—do the initial and final masses agree.

Activity 9.3 further verifies the law using sodium sulfate and barium chloride solutions: when mixed, a white precipitate of barium sulfate and sodium chloride forms, yet the total mass of both flasks is unchanged. The Law of Conservation of Mass, proposed by Antoine Lavoisier in 1789, states that matter can neither be created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction. The section includes two worked examples: one verifying the law numerically for calcium carbonate reacting with hydrochloric acid, and another applying it proportionally to calculate carbon dioxide produced when carbon burns. (Think as a Scientist) Students design and perform their own experiment using zinc and dilute hydrochloric acid to test whether mass is conserved during that reaction, using a set-up of their own choice.

9.2 Law of Constant Proportions

This section introduces Joseph Proust's Law of Constant Proportions (also called the Law of Definite Proportions or Proust's Law), which states that in any compound formed by two or more elements, the elements combine in a fixed ratio by mass regardless of the compound's source. The key example is water: purified water from rivers, borewells, or the ocean always contains hydrogen and oxygen in a mass ratio of 1:8, so 9 g of water always yields 1 g of hydrogen and 8 g of oxygen on decomposition. A worked example applies the law to sodium chloride, in which sodium and chlorine are always in a mass ratio of 23:35.5, to find how much chlorine reacts with 46 g of sodium. (Threads of Curiosity) Students read that cinnabar—known in ancient India as hingula—always yields mercury and sulfur in mass percentages of approximately 86.22% and 13.78% regardless of which civilisation processed it, illustrating the law through a historical cross-cultural example.

9.3 Dalton's Atomic Theory

This section explains how the two laws of Section 9.1 and 9.2 provided the experimental foundation for Dalton's Atomic Theory, which offers a particle-level explanation: atoms are indivisible and merely rearrange during reactions rather than being created or destroyed, thus accounting for conservation of mass; and atoms of a given element are identical so they always combine in the same fixed ratios, thus accounting for constant proportions. John Dalton's postulates, presented in 1808, state that all matter is made of very tiny particles called atoms that participate in chemical reactions; atoms are indivisible and cannot be created or destroyed; atoms of a given element are identical in mass and chemical properties; atoms of different elements have different masses and chemical properties; atoms combine in simple whole-number ratios to form compounds; and the relative number and kinds of atoms are constant in a given compound. Examples used to illustrate the postulates include hydrogen and oxygen combining to form water without the atoms being destroyed, and magnesium burning in air to form magnesium oxide. (What if...) Students consider how the substances around us would change if atoms could combine in any ratio rather than fixed whole-number ratios, reflecting on the significance of Dalton's postulates.

9.4 How Atoms Combine?

Atoms of an element can combine with each other to form molecules of that element, while atoms of different elements combine to form molecules of compounds. A molecule is defined as an electrically neutral entity consisting of more than one atom that is capable of independent existence and shows all the properties of that substance; some elements like helium exist only as atoms because they are already stable. The section recalls from Chapter 8 that atoms with eight electrons in the valence shell (or two electrons if the K-shell is outermost) are stable, and atoms with fewer valence electrons may share, gain, or lose electrons to attain stability. This combining happens in two broad ways: sharing of electrons (covalent bond) and transfer of electrons (ionic bond). When atoms combine, the total energy of the system becomes lower than the sum of individual atomic energies, making the arrangement more stable; the force holding atoms together is called a chemical bond.

9.4.1 Bonding by sharing of electrons — Covalent Bond

A. Molecules of elements

This sub-section explains covalent bond formation in molecules where both atoms are of the same element. For hydrogen (atomic number 1), the single electron in the K-shell means each atom needs one more electron; two hydrogen atoms therefore share one electron each to form H₂, a single bond depicted as H—H. For chlorine (atomic number 17), each atom has seven valence electrons and needs one more; two chlorine atoms share one electron each to form Cl₂, also a single bond (Cl—Cl). For oxygen (atomic number 8), each atom has six valence electrons and needs two more; two oxygen atoms share two electrons each to form O₂, resulting in a double bond depicted as O=O.

B. Molecules of compounds

When atoms of two different elements combine, they still share electrons to satisfy the octet rule. For hydrogen chloride (HCl): hydrogen needs one electron and chlorine needs one, so they share one electron each, forming a single covalent bond (H—Cl). For water (H₂O): oxygen needs two electrons while each hydrogen needs one, so two hydrogen atoms each share one electron with the same oxygen atom, forming two single bonds. The section also introduces the Bridging Science and Society content about atomic/nuclear energy, noting that nuclear energy plays a vital role in electricity generation, medicine, and research; India's contributions to nuclear energy include the work of Raja Ramanna, called the Father of the Indian Nuclear Programme.

C. Naming covalent compounds

Covalent compounds are named using a prefix system that indicates the number of atoms of each element. The first element retains its regular name while the second ends in -ide; prefixes include mono- (1), di- (2), tri- (3), tetra- (4), penta- (5), hexa- (6). Mono- is typically omitted for the first element but used for the second; vowel-dropping rules apply when a prefix ending in 'o' or 'a' meets an element starting with a vowel (e.g. monoxide), but prefixes ending in 'i' are retained (e.g. dioxide). Worked examples include CO (carbon monoxide), CO₂ (carbon dioxide), CS₂ (carbon disulfide), PCl₃ (phosphorus trichloride), SF₆ (sulfur hexafluoride), N₂O₄ (dinitrogen tetroxide), and N₂O₅ (dinitrogen pentoxide). A special rule applies to hydrogen as the first element: no prefix is added regardless of the number of hydrogen atoms, so H₂S is named hydrogen sulfide. Common names like water (H₂O) and ammonia (NH₃) are noted as exceptions that override systematic names.

9.4.2 Bonding by electron transfer — Ionic bond

This sub-section explains bond formation by electron transfer. Atoms whose valence shells have fewer than four electrons generally donate those electrons to achieve stability, forming positively charged cations; atoms with more than four valence electrons gain or share electrons to complete their octet, with the gainers forming anions. The formation of sodium chloride (NaCl) is the central example: sodium (atomic number 11) has one valence electron, loses it to become Na⁺ (11 protons, 10 electrons); chlorine (atomic number 17) has seven valence electrons, gains one to become Cl⁻ (17 protons, 18 electrons). Cations and anions are collectively called ions. The electrostatic force of attraction between oppositely charged ions is called an ionic bond. The section also notes through a Threads of Curiosity inset that ionic compounds typically form three-dimensional crystals rather than individual molecules: in NaCl, each Na⁺ is surrounded by six Cl⁻ and vice versa, arranged in a repeating 3-D crystal lattice structure.

A. Naming ionic compounds

Ionic compounds are named by writing the cation name first followed by the anion name; simple anions end in -ide. Metals generally form cations and non-metals form anions. Polyatomic ions—formed from two or more elements—generally do not end in -ide. Table 9.1 lists common monoatomic ions (Na⁺, Li⁺, K⁺, Ag⁺, Ca²⁺, Ba²⁺, Fe²⁺, Fe³⁺, Cu⁺, Cu²⁺, Mg²⁺, Zn²⁺, Al³⁺, F⁻, Cl⁻, Br⁻, I⁻, O²⁻, S²⁻) and common polyatomic ions (OH⁻, NO₃⁻, HCO₃⁻, CO₃²⁻, SO₄²⁻, NH₄⁺) with their formulae and valencies.

9.5 Writing Chemical Formulae

This section introduces the criss-cross method as a faster way to write formulae without working through electron configurations.

9.5.1 Writing chemical formulae of covalent compounds

The steps are: write the element symbols, write their valencies below each, and criss-cross the valencies as subscripts. If the valency after criss-crossing is one, it is not written. Worked examples include HCl (valencies 1 and 1 → HCl), H₂S (valencies 1 and 2 → H₂S), and CCl₄ (valencies 4 and 1 → CCl₄).

9.5.2 Writing chemical formulae of ionic compounds

The steps are: write the cation symbol first, then the anion; write the charges (not as superscripts but beneath the symbols); criss-cross only the numbers; divide subscripts by any common factor to get the simplest ratio. Worked examples: CaCl₂ (Ca²⁺ and Cl⁻), Al₂O₃ (Al³⁺ and O²⁻), MgO (Mg²⁺ and O²⁻—equal valencies simplify to 1:1), CaCO₃ (Ca²⁺ and CO₃²⁻), Mg(OH)₂ (Mg²⁺ and OH⁻—brackets used for polyatomic ions appearing more than once), Al(OH)₃, and Al₂(SO₄)₃. The rule that charges on ions are not shown in the formula of the compound is noted.

9.6 Properties of the Ionic and the Covalent Compounds

Activity 9.4 is a two-part class experiment comparing solubility and electrical conductivity of camphor, sodium chloride, copper sulfate, sugar, and naphthalene in water, kerosene, and petrol, and in solid and dissolved states. Students group compounds by similar behaviour and draw conclusions. Ionic compounds (NaCl, CuSO₄) are generally soluble in water but insoluble in kerosene and petrol; covalent compounds (camphor, naphthalene) are generally insoluble in water but dissolve in organic solvents. Ionic compounds do not conduct electricity in the solid state because ions are held in fixed positions, but they do conduct when dissolved in water because ions are free to move. Covalent compounds do not provide ions in solution (e.g. sugar dissolves in water but does not conduct), and non-polar covalent compounds like camphor and naphthalene neither dissolve in water nor conduct. Ionic compounds have high melting and boiling points due to strong inter-ionic attractions; covalent compounds generally have low melting and boiling points. (Activity 9.4) Students set up a conductivity circuit with electrodes, a 9 V battery, and a bulb, test each of the five compounds in solid form and in aqueous solution, and record all observations in Table 9.2 before grouping compounds by shared properties.

9.7 Molecular Mass of Covalent Compounds

Molecular mass is the total mass of a molecule, calculated by adding the atomic masses of all atoms in the molecular formula. Worked Example 9.4 calculates the molecular mass of water: H = 1 u, O = 16 u, so H₂O = (1 × 2) + (16 × 1) = 18 u. Worked Example 9.5 calculates the molecular mass of carbon dioxide: C = 12 u, O = 16 u, so CO₂ = (12 × 1) + (16 × 2) = 44 u. The section notes that ionic compounds do not form molecules because their ions arrange in 3-D crystals; molecular mass therefore applies only to covalent compounds.

9.8 Formula Unit Mass of Ionic Compounds

Since ionic compounds do not form molecules, the relevant mass unit is the formula unit mass, which is the mass of one formula unit — the simplest whole-number ratio of ions. Formula unit mass is calculated by adding the atomic masses of all atoms in the formula unit. Worked Example 9.6 calculates the formula unit mass of sodium oxide: Na = 23 u, O = 16 u, so Na₂O = (23 × 2) + (16 × 1) = 62 u. Worked Example 9.7 calculates the formula unit mass of calcium nitrate, Ca(NO₃)₂: Ca = 40 u, N = 14 u, O = 16 u, giving (40 × 1) + {(14 × 1) + (16 × 3)} × 2 = 164 u.

The chapter also connects atomic and nuclear science to India's development, highlighting that nuclear energy from atomic reactions powers electricity generation, medicine, scientific research, and space exploration through thermal energy driving steam turbines. India's own nuclear energy programme, developed with significant contributions from Raja Ramanna, promotes the peaceful use of this science for national development.

ARUVI · LESSON PLAN GENERATION CONSTITUTION · SCIENCE · SECONDARY STAGE · VERSION 1.1

THE SELF-CONTAINED REGISTER (binds Rules 7 and 10)
Three things no time band or teacher note may do, each because the platform enforces it:
1. NAME A CLOCK QUANTITY — the platform scales every band's minutes in proportion to the sitting that carries it, so a stated number is falsified silently: no "for three minutes", "the remaining time", "half the session". 3. NAME CALENDAR TIME — Aruvi keeps no calendar and sittings do not map to days: today, yesterday, this week, next class are unknowable at authoring.

RULE 1 · SECTION ANCHORING — THE ORGANIZING SPINE

MANDATE
Every activity MUST be anchored to a named section of the Chapter Summary. The
section's content — not the competency statement, not the dissolution test
sentence — is the content vehicle for the activity.

The lesson plan follows the chapter summary's own section order. Periods are
assigned to sections in the sequence the sections appear in the chapter. Where
the chapter's own sequence carries a natural build, that build is preserved as
the chapter gives it.

The ordering principle is therefore source-given, not designed: take the order
the chapter already has. Do NOT invent, super-impose, or re-engineer an
ordering the chapter does not itself present — whether a concrete-to-abstract
ramp, a low-to-high cognitive-demand ramp, or a prerequisite arc. Cognitive
demand is read off each section as it stands; it is neither smoothed into a
rising curve nor flagged as a defect when it does not rise.

PROHIBITION
1. MUST NOT include any activity whose content cannot be traced to a specific
   named section of the Chapter Summary.
2. MUST NOT use the competency statement or dissolution test sentence as a
   content source for activities.
3. MUST NOT re-order, skip, or compress sections to fit a narrative shape the
   chapter does not itself contain.

================================================================================
RULE 2 · CONTENT-DRIVEN CALIBRATION

MANDATE
Use the Chapter Summary's own vocabulary, examples, and the cognitive demand of
each section as the age-appropriateness signal. Where complexity signals are
mixed within a section, the cognitive demand of the implied task takes
precedence over surface vocabulary.

Secondary-stage Science content is frequently abstract by nature — reasoning
about what cannot be directly observed, model-based explanation, symbolic and
mathematical representation. A section that involves no hands-on activity is
normal at this stage and MUST NOT be treated as deficient or padded with
invented practical work.

PROHIBITION
MUST NOT adjust or retrieve grade-level calibration from the Pedagogy document.
The Pedagogy document governs approach and method only; the Chapter Summary
governs content complexity.

================================================================================
RULE 3 · PEDAGOGICAL COGNITIVE FLOOR

MANDATE
Every activity MUST require students to do something with the section's
content — observe, classify, explain, reason from evidence, model, represent,
calculate, apply, or construct — at the level the Pedagogy document specifies.

Symbolic, mathematical, and diagrammatic work counts fully as "doing" at this
stage. Where a section's substance is the use of a rule, formula, notation, or
representation (for example shell-filling, mass/atomic number, weighted
averages, equations of motion, ray or circuit diagrams), an activity built on
that representation satisfies the floor on its own. It MUST NOT be judged
incomplete for lacking a hands-on or laboratory component, and a practical
activity MUST NOT be invented to stand in for it.

PROHIBITION
1. MUST NOT satisfy an activity through recall-only tasks (state, name, recall,
   list, define).
2. MUST NOT treat the competency code as the activity target. The competency
   code is a destination, not a task description.

================================================================================
RULE 4 · FULL-SECTION COVERAGE

MANDATE
Across the period budget, every substantive section of the Chapter Summary
MUST receive at least one activity. A section may span more than one period
where its content warrants it; emphasis follows the substance of the section,
not any external score.

If the section count exceeds the available period budget, produce the best
possible plan that covers the chapter in section order AND include a
section_coverage_note in the JSON naming the sections that could not be
allotted their own period.

PROHIBITION
1. MUST NOT apply any numerical allocation formula across sections.
2. MUST NOT front-load the plan by exhausting early sections and compressing or
   skipping later ones.
3. MUST NOT leave a substantive section without at least one activity except
   under a genuine budget shortfall recorded in section_coverage_note.

================================================================================
RULE 5 · PEDAGOGICAL APPROACH DIVERSITY

MANDATE
Draw pedagogical approaches exclusively from the attached Pedagogy document for
Science, Secondary Stage. Each period's approach MUST be justified by the
content of its anchored section — the match between section content and
approach must be defensible.

Each period MUST record exactly one pedagogical_approach as a named field in its
period object (Amendment A3) — the single dominant approach of that period's
activity, named exactly as written in the attached Pedagogy document.

PROHIBITION
1. MUST NOT repeat the same approach across more than two consecutive periods.
2. MUST NOT use approach categories outside the attached Pedagogy document.
3. MUST NOT choose an approach for variety alone.
4. MUST NOT leave pedagogical_approach blank, and MUST NOT list more than one
   approach in the field — record the single dominant approach only.

================================================================================
RULE 6 · INVERTED LO FLOW — ONE IMPLIED LO + SECTION CONTEXT PER SECTION

MANDATE
Generate exactly one implied_lo and one section_context per anchored section,
emitted in the Coverage Handoff array (Rule 9 · Amendment A4), never inside a
period object.

implied_lo — the transferable skill this section develops, stated
independently of chapter content. Format: "Students can [observable skill verb
phrase]." Derivation test: what can the student now do that they could apply
equally in a different chapter?

section_context — a compact label of 10–12 words naming the specific phenomena,
models, quantities, or structures this section drew from. This is what the
assessment question is about. Name the key items only; do not inventory the
whole section.

The assessment generator reads both together from the Coverage Handoff:
implied_lo drives cognitive demand; section_context drives content.

PROHIBITION
1. MUST NOT generate more than one implied_lo per section.
2. MUST NOT place implied_lo, section_context, or any competency field inside a
   period object. These belong exclusively in the Coverage Handoff array
   (Amendment A4) — never duplicated per period.
3. MUST NOT retrieve or reference any Learning Outcome document. LOs are outputs
   of activity design, not inputs.
4. MUST NOT write LOs that restate the competency or dissolution test, or use
   internal-state verbs ("understand", "appreciate"). Use observable verbs only.
5. MUST NOT include chapter-specific proper nouns (named scientists, models,
   elements, organelles) in implied_lo — they belong in section_context.

================================================================================
RULE 7 · TEACHER-FACING TEXT — NO INTERNAL MACHINERY

MANDATE
The lesson plan is read by teachers. All teacher-facing text MUST be written in
plain language a teacher can act on directly.

The teacher-facing fields bound by this rule are:

Refer to chapter content by its plain name and the section it sits in. Where it
helps a teacher locate the material, name the section heading the activity draws

Teacher-facing text MUST NOT expose internal planning machinery. Specifically,

1. Competency codes (C-codes), CG codes, or the dissolution test sentence.
2. Rule numbers or any reference to this constitution.

The competency fields in the Coverage Handoff (Amendment A4) are structured
metadata, not teacher-facing text, and are exempt — but their contents MUST NOT
leak into any of the teacher-facing fields named above.

`homework` per period is `[]` by default. Populate with 1–2 items only
when in-class time-box overflows or when reinforcement is judged useful.
Homework is not consumed by the assessment generator downstream.

Homework is not owned by any actor — it is a bridge between periods,

RULE 9 · COVERAGE HANDOFF — REQUIRED COMPANION OUTPUT

At the close of the lesson plan, produce the Coverage Handoff as a JSON array

- LOs are outputs only. No LO document is an input.
- TIME: the schedule is a single standard row. Total minutes = duration × count.
  Total period count = count. Each period has exactly one activity calibrated to
  the standard duration. MUST NOT exceed total period count. The full budget is teaching
  only — no period budget is reserved for assessment, and no assessment task,
  question, or time estimate is embedded in the lesson plan.
- Section anchoring (Rule 1) is absolute — no exceptions for introductory,
  transition, or review activities.
- ITEM ANCHORING IS DERIVED, NOT DECLARED: an assessment item's anchor unit is
  resolved by the platform from its section_number through this handoff's
  period_numbers. MUST NOT emit period_ref (or any unit number) on an assessment
  item — at this stage the unique link is the SECTION, and a section may be taught
  across several units (Rule 4).

================================================================================
AMENDMENT A3 — FULL LP JSON SCHEMA

The system MUST populate every field. Empty strings and empty arrays are not
permitted for required fields. Field constraints (do not violate):
- visual_aids: the visual resource the activity needs (textbook figure, board
  diagram, model, SVG figure); null if none. Do not invent requirements.
- activity_title: teacher-facing label, 10–13 words; not a sentence — no trailing
  period, subtitle, or chapter-specific code.
- pedagogical_approach: exactly one approach copied verbatim from the Pedagogy
  document (Rule 5); never blank, never more than one.
- section_coverage_note: present only under Rule 4's budget shortfall; else null.
- period_schedule: exactly one row — the class-standard duration × count (INPUTS 4).

Period objects carry teaching mechanics only — implied_lo, section_context and
c_code live in coverage_handoff (Amendment A4), not in any period object. cg is
emitted once at the top level as chapter_cg (below), never per section.

=== ASSESSMENT CONSTITUTION ===
ARUVI · CHAPTER ASSESSMENT GENERATION CONSTITUTION · SCIENCE · SECONDARY STAGE · VERSION 1.2

Subject group : science
Stage         : Secondary Stage   ·   Grades : ix · x
Task          : assessment_generation
Upstream      : lesson_plan_constitution_science (Secondary) — coverage_handoff (Amendment A4)
Inputs        : coverage_handoff + Chapter Summary (exactly two; both required)

================================================================================
RULE 1 · GOVERNING PURPOSE

MANDATE
Generate tasks that test whether the student can perform the cognitive operation
each section develops. Every question MUST trace to the implied_lo of the section
it tests, and require an observable demonstration — response, product,
classification, or justification.

PROHIBITION
1. No questions asking whether a student understood, appreciated, or felt
   something — demonstration, not self-report.
2. MUST NOT test content absorption independently of the section's implied_lo.
3. MUST NOT derive any architectural decision (length, format, ordering) from a
   section's position in the chapter.

================================================================================
RULE 2 · INPUTS AND OUTPUTS

INPUTS (two, both required)
1. coverage_handoff — from the Secondary LP (Amendment A4). One entry per anchored
   section: section_number, section_label, total_sections, period_numbers,
   period_duration_minutes, activity_summary, implied_lo, section_context, c_code,
   co_central. The parent Curricular Goal arrives once at chapter level (chapter_cg
   in the LP JSON), NOT per section. Read as committed — do NOT re-derive,
   re-order, or supplement.
   · Emit chapter_cg once at chapter level, never per question. c_code is kept per
     question (the LP permits complementary C-codes, so it may vary by section).
2. Chapter Summary — structured content mirroring textbook headings. Supplies the
   actual phenomena, examples, values, structures, and misconception material
   that ground each question (Rule 3).

OUTPUTS (three, all mandatory)
1. Section-structured assessment, items in coverage_handoff order.
2. Diagnostically intentional MCQ distractors (Rule 7).
3. A guide block per question (Rule 9), structured JSON, visible on demand.

PROHIBITION
MUST NOT reference the Curricular Goals doc, Chapter Mapping JSON, Pedagogy doc,
any LO document, or any source outside the two inputs; MUST NOT re-evaluate
competencies, re-open mapping, or alter the committed coverage_handoff.

================================================================================
RULE 3 · CONTENT GROUNDING — TAG SHAPES · CONTEXT SCOPES · SUMMARY SUPPLIES

MANDATE — three roles, never conflated:
  · cognitive_demand (Rule 4) SHAPES the item — question type and depth (Rule 5).
  · section_context SCOPES the item — names and fences it to one slice of the
    chapter. It is a label, not content.
  · the section's Chapter Summary slice SUPPLIES the item — the real examples,
    values, structures, and misconception material for the stem, visual_stimulus,
    correct answer, and distractors.
A question built from section_context alone, without the summary's concrete
material, is non-compliant.

ADJACENT PULL (bounded)
Each item is OWNED BY and TESTS exactly one section. The correct answer and the
tested operation MUST come from that section's own slice. Neighbouring-section
material may be pulled ONLY as supporting scaffold — a distractor exploiting a
genuine cross-section confusion, or a scenario needing a neighbouring fact — never
as the thing assessed. "Which section does this test?" MUST have one answer.

================================================================================
RULE 4 · COGNITIVE DEMAND TAG — THE GOVERNING HINGE

MANDATE
For every section, classify it on the Recall–Understanding–Application–Analysis–
Evaluation spectrum and record the result as cognitive_demand on every question
for that section. This tag is the single governor of format (Rule 5). It MUST be
derived from and consistent with the section's implied_lo and summary slice — it
makes the LP's demand explicit and auditable, never reopening or recalibrating it.

Reading guide (operation, not position):
  identify · name · state · recognise · recall            → Recall
  describe · explain (one-step) · represent · classify    → Understanding
  calculate · apply · balance · determine · use…to find   → Application
  compare · analyse · infer · distinguish · explain why   → Analysis
  evaluate · justify · judge · critique · decide between  → Evaluation
Where vocabulary and implied task conflict, the implied task's demand governs.

PROHIBITION
MUST NOT assign the tag from position or from neighbouring sections; MUST NOT
leave it blank or use a value outside the five-point spectrum.

================================================================================
RULE 5 · DEMAND-TO-FORMAT MATCHING

MANDATE — format follows the tag, never position:
  Recall / Understanding     → MCQ        (determinate answer; errors diagnosable
                                            via distractors, Rule 7)
  Application                → SCR        (correct multi-step chain; the steps are
                                            the object, so selection can't reveal them)
  Analysis / Evaluation      → ECR        (no single answer; quality lives in the
                                            written reasoning)
  Integrative / cross-       → OPEN_TASK  (several operations on a novel scenario;
  operational (co_central)                 vehicle from the Science menu, Rule 8)

co_central = true: a section integrating both central operations is the OPEN_TASK
and MUST require reasoning across both at once (Rule 8).

PER-SECTION COUNT (demand-sized, may mix)
Count follows section substance, mirroring the LP's full-section-coverage logic.
A rich section MAY carry more than one item and MAY mix types (e.g. MCQ on a fact
+ SCR on the procedure); a thin section gets one item of its band. NO fixed
minimum, NO mandatory MCQ count. An anchor MCQ accompanies an extended item ONLY
where the section has determinate factual content worth a separate check — never
by default.

EXPECTED BUDGET (guidance, not a cap)
Length is uncapped, but target ≈ one item per section, a second only on genuinely
rich sections, and at most one open task. "Rich" is a substantive judgment — a
second item is warranted only when one cannot capture distinct, separately
testable content. MUST NOT treat most sections as rich; quiet doubling of length
is the failure this guards against.

PROHIBITION
MUST NOT assign format from position, from the implied_lo type as a label, or for
variety; MUST NOT impose a uniform count or fixed MCQ minimum; MUST NOT pair an
anchor MCQ with every extended item by default.

================================================================================
RULE 6 · REASONING FLOOR

MANDATE
The assessment as a whole MUST contain at least one extended-reasoning item (one
ECR or one OPEN_TASK), guarding against a recognition-only assessment on a
procedural chapter. If no section reaches Analysis, Evaluation, or the integrative
band, lift the single highest-demand section to ECR (or OPEN_TASK only where the
chapter genuinely integrates operations), and note the lift in that guide block.

PROHIBITION
MUST NOT emit an all-MCQ/SCR assessment; MUST NOT lift more than one section; MUST
NOT manufacture integration a chapter lacks — ECR is the default lift.

================================================================================
RULE 7 · MCQ DISTRACTOR DESIGN

MANDATE
Every MCQ has exactly three diagnostic distractors (four options). Each is one
nameable engagement failure: a misconception about the section; a confusion
between two chapter concepts (same or adjacent section per Rule 3); or recall of a
related-but-wrong detail from the section's slice.
Option order carries no meaning and is not yours to set: emit the four options in
whatever order they were authored, and never let where an option sits influence how
it is written. Uneven letters across a chapter are coincidence, not a defect.

PROHIBITION
1. No true/false; no implausible, arbitrary, or out-of-chapter distractors.
2. MUST NOT write an option that refers to another option by its label ("both A and
   B", "none of the above") — options are ordered downstream and a label reference
   would be falsified.

================================================================================
RULE 8 · OPEN TASK MENU — SCIENCE

MANDATE
Where Rule 5 or 6 calls for an OPEN_TASK, select its format ONLY from this menu,
justify the choice in the guide block, and state that the teacher may substitute
any other menu format. Each format is self-contained and classroom-answerable
(Rule 10):
  · Data interpretation (provided table or graph)
  · Classification / sorting with justification
  · Procedure evaluation (identify flaw, suggest improvement)
  · Diagram completion and annotation
  · Predict-and-explain
co_central = true: the single OPEN_TASK is the integrative demonstration of both
operations and MUST NOT be split.

PROHIBITION
No format outside the menu; no selection for variety (it must be the most natural
vehicle for the section's implied_lo); never more than one OPEN_TASK per
assessment.

================================================================================
RULE 9 · GUIDE LAYER

MANDATE
Produce a guide block per question, as structured JSON (not prose), visible on
demand. By type:
  MCQ        — guide.MCQ.what_each_option_reveals (one entry per non-correct
               option, naming its engagement failure) · inclusivity.
  SCR        — expected_elements (top-level: components a complete response needs)
               · guide.SCR: learning_outcome{section} · inclusivity.
  ECR        — look_for (top-level: markers of a strong response)
               · guide.ECR: learning_outcome{section} · inclusivity.
  OPEN_TASK  — guide.OPEN_TASK: format_type · format_rationale ·
               what_this_demonstrates · reading_the_scaffold ·
               strong_vs_weak_markers · inclusivity · learning_outcome{section}.

inclusivity is REQUIRED in every guide block, all four types: 1–2 sentences on the
alternative pathways by which different students demonstrate the same outcome.
learning_outcome.section records the section_number tested. A Rule 6 lift MUST be
noted in its guide block.

PROHIBITION
MUST NOT omit the guide block, or render it as prose.

================================================================================
RULE 10 · EXECUTABILITY BOUNDARY

MANDATE
Every task MUST be answerable by a student working alone in a classroom, using
only what the question provides. The assessment is NOT timetabled into the
chapter's period budget (that belongs to the LP), so this boundary governs
COORDINATION and SELF-CONTAINMENT, not clock time: no field visits, external
speakers, community involvement, or externally-sourced materials.

NOTE
Secondary Science is often abstract — model-based reasoning, symbolic/mathematical
representation, diagram and equation work all count fully as student output. A
task MUST NOT be judged deficient for lacking a hands-on component.

PROHIBITION
No multi-session projects, field visits, craft-material artefacts, or
out-of-classroom coordination.

================================================================================
RULE 11 · SCOPE BOUNDARY

Chapter-scoped formative assessment only. MUST NOT generate summative/Board-prep
assessments, Holistic Progress Card inputs, multi-session projects or portfolios,
or cross-chapter student tracking.

================================================================================
INTEGRITY CONSTRAINTS (system level — override any other instruction)

· coverage_handoff is committed — no reopening competencies or re-deriving fields.
· Position carries no signal — no format, count, or ordering may derive from it.
· cognitive_demand (Rule 4) is the sole format governor, consistent with implied_lo.
· section_number is internal (generation + guide block); never in user-facing output.
· ANCHORING: section_number IS the item's anchor. The platform resolves it to the
  unit(s) that teach the section through the LP's coverage_handoff period_numbers;
  MUST NOT emit period_ref or any unit number on an item.
· Content grounding (Rule 3): summary supplies, section_context scopes — neither
  substitutes the other.
· Executability (Rule 10): every task self-contained and classroom-answerable; the
  assessment has no clock-time budget of its own.

================================================================================
AMENDMENT A1 — FULL ASSESSMENT JSON SCHEMA (SCIENCE · SECONDARY)

Output a JSON object conforming exactly to this schema — the single source of
truth for online display and PDF generation. Populate every field; empty strings
and empty arrays are not permitted for required fields.

  VS-1 · Required: if the student must read a data table (results grid, readings,

    header.
  VS-2 · It holds the real rows and columns, not a prose description. "A data
    table is provided with columns X, Y, Z" is prohibited.
  VS-3 · question_text / task / scaffold only reference it ("Refer to the table

  VS-4 · null only when the question genuinely needs no table/diagram. Saying "the

  Diagrams: a question may need an SVG figure (circuit, ray diagram, structural

STANDARD CANONICAL BRIEF — 18 periods (platform-computed; binding)

- This is the chapter's fullest plan: 18 units x 50 minutes (period_schedule: exactly one row {50, 18}).
- ITS UNITS ARE SERVED WHOLE AND IN PARTS. A teacher whose budget differs receives another plan's first X-1 units followed by ONE unit borrowed from this plan — the unit that FIRST introduces the section her class has reached. So ANY unit of this plan may be somebody's last sitting, met by a class that never had the units before it.
- Therefore every unit CLOSES ON ITS OWN GROUND. Write each unit as though it were the only sitting this class receives: it stands up on the material it teaches inside its own minutes. Where continuity helps, name the CONTENT already taught — the idea, text, method or phenomenon — never a unit's position or existence.
- THE SERVE MODEL IS NEVER THE TEACHER'S BUSINESS. Everything above constrains how you BUILD the plan; none of it is a subject the plan may discuss. Do not reassure the teacher that a unit assumes no prior draft, requires no earlier activity, needs no particular sitting to have happened, or stands alone — simply write a unit of which those things are true. State what THIS sitting does; say nothing about what it does not need. If a sentence would be pointless to a teacher who had never heard of variant plans, cut it.
- MATERIALS, OPENING MOVES AND HOMEWORK ARE PER-UNIT. No unit may require that another unit was taught, or that its homework was set, in order to run.
- NO UNIT MAY DEPEND ON A PHYSICAL ARTEFACT ANOTHER UNIT PRODUCES. If a unit needs a poster, chart, model, collection or draft to exist, it must make it itself within its own minutes, or the material must be something any classroom already has. A unit that lists 'prepared previously', 'their charts from earlier' or 'the models they built' in `materials`, `visual_aids` or an opening band is asking for a sitting that may not have happened — it is the same failure as naming another unit, arriving through the props instead of the prose. Where the chapter genuinely wants a make-then-present pair, put BOTH acts inside ONE unit. A STUDENT'S OWN PIECE OF WRITING COUNTS: an article, essay, letter or story drafted in one unit and continued, revised or finished in another is the same dependency in a thinner disguise. Plan every writing task to begin AND end inside a single unit — drafting, peer response and revision together, on a scale that fits the minutes available.
- THE SYNTHESIS MANDATE (this plan alone carries it): unit 18, the final unit, is a WHOLE-CHAPTER SYNTHESIS and its section_anchor is exactly the single word: synthesis (the reserved token — NOT a section name, no joining). It draws the entire chapter together as a real unit-arc. It may assume every SECTION'S CONTENT has been taught, and may connect back to concepts BY NAME — but it must NOT assume any particular earlier activity, reading, discussion, homework or material actually happened: it will be served to classes that covered the same sections through DIFFERENT units.
- THE SYNTHESIS UNIT STARTS AND FINISHES ITS OWN WORK. It may DRAW ON what the chapter taught; it must not CONTINUE, complete, revise or hand back a piece of student work another unit began — no 'complete the draft', no 'finish the poster', no 'return to the essay you started'. A borrowing class may have done that work in one sitting, or in a different form, or not yet at all. Any writing, making or performing in this unit begins and ends inside its own minutes.
- COVERAGE COMPLETES BEFORE THE SYNTHESIS: all registry sections first-appear across units 1..17. No other unit may use the synthesis token.
- GIVE THE SYNTHESIS UNIT ITS OWN coverage_handoff ROW. At this stage an assessment item names a GROUP (its section number), never a unit, and the platform resolves the unit from that group's handoff row — so a unit with no row can hold no question. Emit one final handoff entry for unit 18: the next number in sequence, its period_numbers exactly [18], its title/ref the word synthesis (this is the ONE row whose label is not copied from the chapter summary, because the unit is not a section), and its implied_lo the integrative outcome the closing sitting actually builds. Then write its items against that row like any other. Do NOT count this row in total_sections — that is the number of SECTIONS the chapter has, and synthesis is not one of them.
- Save as: ch_10_canonical.json

=== PEDAGOGY DOCUMENT ===
National Curriculum Framework for School Education
4.4.2.2 Secondary Stage — Science Pedagogy Context
4.6.1 Pedagogy for Science


4.6.1 Pedagogy for Science

Learning Science involves not just learning theories and facts of Science, but also making
connections between conceptual learning and real life, acquiring the capacities of scientific
inquiry, and most importantly, applying these to understanding the world.

Students like to explore the world around them and understand why and how things happen. In
this process of exploration, they use trial-and-error methods to test their hypotheses and reach
possible conclusions. This exploration need not take place individually — students learn Science
best through engaging with peers and adults.

Students have theories about why things happen, patterns they see around them, and about
cause-and-effect relationships. As they learn about Science in a more formal set-up, these ideas
get tested. Some concepts fit into the students' current understanding, while others require a
shift in thinking. If there is an alignment between current ideas and what is discussed in
classrooms, ideas get strengthened.

At the same time, some concepts do not fit into the students' current thinking. If not addressed,
they can turn into alternative conceptions. For example, heavy objects fall faster, plants are non-
living because they don't move, or heavy/big objects always sink in water. If these ideas are not
challenged and suitably modified through investigation, they can turn into alternative conceptions
which may persist as students move through school.

Apart from these theories, students also bring with them the ability to reason, understand, and
explain relationships between cause and effect. These capacities serve as the basis for developing
scientific reasoning. Opportunities, therefore, to inquire are important, as opposed to being 'told'.
Scientific values, such as honesty and integrity, also develop through 'doing Science'. For example,
while demonstrating an experiment on the boiling point of water, we should write the reading on
the thermometer accurately, even if the water is not boiling at 100 degrees.

The role of the Teacher in aligning pedagogy and assessment with how students learn Science is
critical. Teachers must build an environment that promotes natural curiosity, encourages
questions, gives maximum possible opportunities for hands-on activities, and gives ample space
to discuss ideas. Opportunities for students to express their understanding through different
modes and formative assessments to track growing understanding are also key to learning
Science.

4.6.1.1 Pedagogic Principles

Science pedagogy across stages must be informed by the following principles:

a. Learning Science requires an active engagement of students with the world around them to
   understand it. Science pedagogy achieves this through:
   i.  Simulating the processes of Science such as asking questions, hypothesising, observing,
       testing, finding evidence, collecting data, analysing, modifying conclusions,
       communicating, and re-questioning.
   ii. Exposing students to a variety of aspects of learning Science in varied settings — the
       laboratory, classroom, and field — through approaches such as inquiry, discovery,
       didactic, hands-on Science.
   iii. Encouraging and sustaining curiosity by providing varied experiences that may
        challenge students' existing notions and ideas.

b. Learning Science requires communication and sharing of ideas and observations. Science
   pedagogy achieves this through:
   i.  Using scientific vocabulary during instruction and creating a variety of contexts and
       situations for students to communicate their understanding, ideas, and observations.
   ii. Peer and collaborative learning.

c. Learning Science requires a gradual increase in the capacity to engage with complex and
   abstract ideas, aligned with the cognitive and procedural capacities of students. Science
   pedagogy achieves this by building on students' existing knowledge and using multiple
   representations (mathematical, graphical, diagrammatic, and models).

d. Learning Science requires making linkages between knowledge for the holistic and
   multidisciplinary learning emphasised in NEP 2020. Science pedagogy achieves this
   through:
   i.  Connecting scientific knowledge inside and outside the classroom.
   ii. Horizontal connections with other curricular areas.

e. Learning Science enables the development of certain values, such as collaboration,
   sensitivity, empathy, equality of opportunities, respect for diversity, and other values
   mentioned in NEP 2020. Science pedagogy must facilitate this process.

4.6.1.2 Recommended Pedagogical Approaches and Settings

The same pedagogical approach can be used across the three settings most suitable for learning
Science — the classroom, the field, and the laboratory. The following is a list of considerations
based on which Teachers can choose pedagogical approaches and settings:

a. The nature of a concept should guide the decision regarding the approach and setting.
   For example, speed can be discussed in the playing field, but the structure of a cell
   requires a microscope.
b. The approach and setting chosen should enable the attainment of learning outcomes
   and competencies.
c. Each of the recommended approaches and settings must be selected at least once in an
   academic year, if not more. This will ensure exposure to varied approaches and settings.
d. Even when Teachers choose a didactic approach, areas that students could have
   potentially inquired about or discovered should be highlighted.

a. Hands-on Science
The most important part of learning Science is actually 'doing Science' through hands-on
experiential learning. 'Doing Science' can range from trial and error, using materials around
them, or using basic scientific instruments (measuring instruments), and laboratory apparatus.
In this process, students gain conceptual understanding and develop capacities through
manipulating, designing, and building experiments and demonstrations.

b. Discovery approach
Students explore the natural world following their own interests and discover patterns of
how the world works during their explorations. Teachers may also create opportunities or
draw attention to natural phenomena that students can explore further. Often, this discovery
is followed by other, more structured approaches to ensure learning. For example, the Teacher
draws the attention of the students to changes in the length of the shadows as the day
progresses or to the venation patterns of the leaves of different plants. Students' observations
on shadows are then connected to scientific concepts such as the path of light, and the
venation pattern is connected to the shapes of the leaves.

c. Inquiry approach
The inquiry approach allows students to navigate through unknown questions and explore
solutions on their own. It allows students to work in the same way as scientists. The inquiry
approach engages students with systematic observation, visualising, experimenting, inferring,
communicating, and discovering relations. This approach allows Teachers to choose the
appropriate type of inquiry with respect to the concept and to scaffold (support as per need)
students' learning. For example, students could explore questions such as: How do the image
characteristics vary with the relative position between lens and object? How does the surface
area of the reactants affect the rate of reaction? How does the intensity of light affect the rate
of photosynthesis?

d. Project-centred approach
This approach allows learning within the classroom to continue outside the classroom and
extend over a period of time. For example, observing the changes in the moon over a month
to understand the phases of the moon. In this process, connections to daily life are also made.
The project-centred approach allows students to develop artefacts/products (charts,
presentations, speeches) that reflect and communicate their emerging understanding. It also
allows the integration of concepts across different curricular areas.

e. Didactic approach
Often, teaching Science involves communicating certain important information in the form of
scientific terms, phenomena, and the historical development of concepts and ideas. In this
approach, the Teacher largely regulates the direction and flow of the lesson.

f. Demonstration
The Teacher demonstrates the working of certain instruments or outcomes of experimental
set-ups to draw the attention of the students to relevant concepts. These demonstrations
enrich students' learning experiences of the concepts.

Teacher's Voice 4.6i — Demonstrating Osmosis in Living Cells (Grade 9)
For my Grade 9 students, I planned a demonstration of osmosis in living cells. They already
are familiar with the concept in form of daily life examples such as what causes pruning of
our fingers if kept in water for long, but in this session, we go a level deeper to observe the
process in living cells under the microscope.

We will have a total of 90 minutes to perform this. Hence, I prepare the material such as
common salt (NaCl) solution and cut onion pieces and equipment such as glass slides,
forceps, and microscopes. Students work in multiple groups. Hence, I prepare as many
instruction/observation recording sheets.

On that day, I begin by demonstrating the experiment — I prepare three slides A, B and C,
add drops of solution in varying quantity, place coverslip, and then observe under the
microscope what is happening to the cells in the onion peel on the slide.

Then all groups repeat this same set of actions and record their observation by drawing
on the sheet provided. Post this, we discuss whatever we observed. After the students
discuss possible inferences, I introduce the term 'osmosis' to the class, using the concept
to explain their observations and share more daily life examples where we see this
phenomena — for example, in the process of pickling.

=== CHAPTER SUMMARY ===
Chapter 10: Sound Waves: Characteristics and Applications

10.1 Production of Sound
This section establishes that sound is produced by the vibration of objects. It begins by recalling prior learning about sonority and the role of vibration in producing sound in musical instruments. The key concept introduced is vibration — defined as the periodic to-and-fro (oscillatory) motion of an object — and students learn that sound ceases as soon as vibration stops. The section also notes that sound can be produced by vibrating strings, membranes, air columns, and other vibrating bodies, and that the object producing sound is called the source. In humans, sound is produced by the vibration of vocal cords inside the larynx; the tongue, lips, mouth, and nasal cavity shape this into speech.
(Activity 10.1) Students stretch a rubber band across an open cardboard box, pluck it to observe that sound is produced only while the band vibrates, change tension to observe how the sound changes, and then remove the band from the box to compare loudness — concluding that sound is produced by vibrations.

10.1.1 Tuning fork
A tuning fork is a U-shaped metal bar (steel or aluminium) with a stem; its prongs or tines are struck against a rubber pad to produce vibration. The section explains why a soft pad is used (to avoid damage) and establishes that a vibrating tuning fork confirms the vibration-sound link through two observations: hearing the sound and watching ripples on a water surface when the prong touches it.
(Activity 10.2) Students strike a tuning fork against a rubber pad, hold it near the ear in different orientations to verify sound production, and touch the vibrating prong to a water surface to see waves form — reinforcing that sound arises from vibrating objects.

10.2 Propagation of Sound
This section addresses how sound travels from a vibrating source to a listener and whether it can travel through all states of matter. The material through which sound propagates is defined as the medium. Two successive investigations demonstrate that sound travels through solids and through liquids, extending the earlier understanding that it travels through gases (air).
(Activity 10.3) One student knocks on a desk while the other listens first through the air and then with ear pressed to the desk surface, establishing that sound travels through solids.
(Activity 10.4) Two metal spoons are tapped together first in air, then submerged in a water-filled tub, demonstrating that sound travels through liquids.

10.2.1 Sound needs a medium to propagate
The section uses the vacuum bell jar experiment to demonstrate that sound cannot travel without a medium. An electric bell inside a sealed jar becomes progressively fainter as air is pumped out and is almost inaudible at near-vacuum; sound returns when air is let back in. The section applies this to outer space, explaining why spacewalking astronauts cannot hear each other directly and must use electronic communication devices built into their suits. The conclusion is that sound is a mechanical disturbance requiring a solid, liquid, or gaseous medium to propagate.

10.3 Sound Waves
This section explains how sound propagates mechanically through a medium using two analogies: a slinky and an oscillating piston in a tube. The slinky analogy shows that a disturbance travels along the spring as regions of closely spaced and widely spaced turns (compressions and rarefactions), while the marked coil itself only oscillates back and forth about its position — it does not travel with the wave. Applying this to air: a forward-moving piston compresses nearby air particles, creating a region of higher-than-average density called a compression (C); a backward-moving piston creates a lower-density region called a rarefaction (R). Alternate compressions and rarefactions propagate through the air as a sound wave. The disturbance (not the particles) travels outward. In an open medium, sound spreads in all directions as spherical waves from a point source. Sound waves are longitudinal waves — particles of the medium vibrate parallel to the direction of wave propagation. Since they require a material medium, sound waves are classified as mechanical waves.
(Activity 10.5) Students lay a marked slinky on a table and push-pull one end rhythmically while a partner holds the other end fixed, observing that compressions and rarefactions travel along the slinky while the marked coil only oscillates about its position — modelling how sound propagates through a medium.

10.4 Energy of Sound Waves
This section establishes that sound is a form of energy by showing that it can do mechanical work on matter at a distance. When a loud sound is produced near a taut membrane stretched over a container with grains sprinkled on it, the grains jump even though the source is not touching the membrane. The explanation is that sound waves transfer energy through the medium by particle vibration and particle collisions; it is the energy, not the medium particles themselves, that is transported. The section introduces microphones (converting sound energy to electrical energy via a vibrating diaphragm) and speakers (doing the reverse) as practical examples of sound energy conversion.
(Activity 10.6) Students stretch a cellophane or rubber sheet over a wide-mouthed container, sprinkle grains evenly on it, and produce loud sounds nearby without touching the container — observing grains move or jump as evidence that sound carries energy.

10.5 Graphical Representation of a Sound Wave
This section introduces the graph of a sound wave as a plot of the density of the medium against distance from the source at a given instant of time. Regions of compression appear as crests (density above average) and rarefactions appear as troughs (density below average). The highest point on the graph is called the crest and the lowest the trough. The section establishes that this graphical form makes it possible to read off wave properties such as wavelength and amplitude visually, preparing students for the quantitative section that follows.

10.6 Characteristics of a Sound Wave

10.6.1 Wavelength, frequency and time period
Three fundamental wave quantities are defined here. Wavelength (λ, SI unit: metre) is the distance between two consecutive crests or two consecutive troughs. Frequency (ν, SI unit: hertz, Hz) is the number of complete density oscillations at a fixed point per unit time; it is what distinguishes musical notes — each note has a distinct frequency. Time period (T, SI unit: second) is the time taken for one complete density oscillation at a fixed point; frequency and time period are inversely related by ν = 1/T. The section notes that everyday sounds contain a mixture of frequencies, while nearly pure single-frequency sounds can be produced by a tuning fork or by whistling. A worked example calculates frequency and time period from oscillation count and duration.
(Activity 10.7 — teacher demonstration) Using the Phyphox app's Audio Spectrum mode, the teacher facilitates students singing musical notes Sa through Ni or using a tone-generating app, observing how frequency changes with each note and recording approximate frequency values — revealing that each note has a distinct frequency and that Sa is the lowest.

10.6.2 Amplitude and intensity of the sound waves
The amplitude of a sound wave is defined as the maximum change in the density of the medium in a compression (or rarefaction) compared to average density; a larger density change corresponds to larger amplitude. A wave with larger amplitude carries more energy than one with smaller amplitude. The intensity of sound is defined as the amount of sound energy passing through a unit area perpendicular to the direction of propagation per unit time. As sound travels away from its source it spreads over a larger area, so the same amount of energy covers more area and intensity decreases with distance. Sounds with larger initial amplitude carry more energy and can travel farther before intensity drops to zero.

10.6.3 Speed of Sound
The speed of sound is defined as the distance a point on a wave (such as a crest) travels per unit time. For a wave of given frequency, one wavelength is covered in one time period, giving the key relation v = λν. The speed of sound depends on the medium: it is fastest in solids, slower in liquids, and slowest in gases — roughly 15–20 times faster in solids and 4–5 times faster in water than in air. Speed in air also increases with temperature and humidity; for example, it is approximately 331 m s⁻¹ in dry air at 0°C and 344 m s⁻¹ at 22°C. In most media, speed depends only on the medium, not on the source or frequency — so if frequency changes, wavelength adjusts while speed stays constant. Several worked examples apply v = λν to calculate wavelengths for the audible range extremes, estimate lightning distance from thunder delay, and find frequency and time period from a graphical representation.
(What if… box) Students are prompted to reason what would happen to the quality of music if the speed of sound in air depended on its frequency — this is a body-text thought prompt classified as a reasoning task.

10.6.4 Human perception of sound
This section distinguishes measurable physical properties from subjective perception. Pitch is how humans perceive frequency: high-frequency sounds are perceived as shrill (high pitch) and low-frequency sounds as deep (low pitch), though the exact mathematical relation is complex. The human audible range is 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz (20 kHz); sounds below 20 Hz are infrasonic waves and those above 20 kHz are ultrasonic waves. Some animals can detect frequencies outside this range — dogs, cats, bats, and dolphins detect ultrasound; elephants detect infrasound. Loudness is how humans perceive amplitude: larger-amplitude sounds are heard as louder; loudness decreases with distance. Intensity is a physical measurement while loudness is subjective and depends on the listener's hearing ability. Sound loudness is measured in decibels (dB). Unwanted or harmful sound is noise; prolonged exposure above safe limits can cause hearing loss, detectable by audiograms, and may be addressed with hearing aids (microphone + amplifier + speaker).
(Activity 10.8 — teacher demonstration) Using a mobile app to generate tones, the teacher leads students from 100 Hz to 1000 Hz in 100 Hz steps and then down toward 20 Hz, having students listen and describe how sound changes with frequency — establishing that higher frequency sounds are perceived as shriller.

10.7 Reflection of Sound
Sound waves bounce off obstacles (solids or liquids) in a manner analogous to light reflection: the incident and reflected sound make equal angles with the normal to the reflecting surface, and all three lie in the same plane. This section frames the laws of reflection for sound and introduces the two most common acoustic consequences — echo and reverberation — that follow from this principle.

10.7.1 Echo
An echo is a reflected sound that reaches the listener after a perceptible time delay. It is produced when sound reflects off a hard, smooth, distant surface such as a mountain, cliff, or long corridor wall. The minimum time interval the human brain requires to perceive two sounds as separate is 0.1 s; if the reflected sound arrives within less than 0.1 s it merges with the original and no distinct echo is heard. Taking the speed of sound as 340 m s⁻¹, the minimum echo distance from a reflecting surface is 17 m (sound must travel to the surface and back, totalling 34 m in 0.1 s). Hard, smooth surfaces produce stronger echoes; soft surfaces absorb and rough surfaces scatter sound, reducing echo clarity. A worked example applies the echo formula to calculate distance from a wall given the delay time.

10.7.2 Reverberation
Reverberation occurs in large enclosed spaces (halls, auditoriums) where sound undergoes multiple reflections from walls and other surfaces. When reflected sounds arrive with time differences of less than 0.05 s, they cannot be distinguished from the original sound and the sound appears to persist after the source has stopped. Reverberation is architecturally managed in modern auditoriums through sound-absorbing panels, upholstered seats, curtains, and porous materials, which reduce unwanted multiple reflections and prevent garbling. A well-designed auditorium achieves controlled reverberation so the audience at all positions hears clear, undistorted sound.

10.8 Ultrasonic and Infrasonic Waves, and their Applications
This section surveys the practical uses of sound at frequencies outside the human audible range. Infrasonic waves (below 20 Hz) are used to detect earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, and severe storms because they travel long distances through both air and the Earth. Ultrasonic waves (above 20 kHz) have a wide range of applications: imaging internal organs without surgery (ultrasonography), breaking kidney stones into smaller fragments that can pass naturally, ultrasonic welding and cleaning of delicate machine parts, non-destructive testing to detect defects inside metal blocks, and locating objects via reflection.

10.8.1 Echolocation
Echolocation is the biological and technological application of reflected sound waves to locate objects. Bats emit short bursts of ultrasonic waves and use the returning echoes to determine the position of obstacles and prey even in complete darkness. Other animals — dolphins, whales, and certain birds — also use echolocation for navigation and hunting. Humans have adapted this principle in sonar (Sound Navigation and Ranging): ultrasonic pulses are transmitted into water and the reflected signals are analysed to determine the distance, direction, and speed of underwater objects such as submarines or shipwrecks. A worked example uses the sonar equation (distance = v × t/2) to calculate depth from echo return time and wave speed.

The chapter connects sound to several real-world applications. Microphones convert sound energy into electrical signals via a vibrating diaphragm, while speakers reverse the process — both illustrating the transformability of sound energy. Noise pollution, measured in decibels, poses significant health risks including hearing loss; hearing aids (comprising a microphone, amplifier, and speaker) help those affected. Audio surveillance using sensitive sound sensors detects drones and aircraft by their characteristic low-frequency signatures, enabling airspace monitoring for safety and security.

You are Aruvi's lesson plan and assessment generator.

You operate under two constitutions that govern every decision you make.
These constitutions are binding. No instruction in the user prompt overrides them.

=== LESSON PLAN GENERATION CONSTITUTION ===
ARUVI · LESSON PLAN GENERATION CONSTITUTION · SCIENCE · SECONDARY STAGE · VERSION 1.1

VOCABULARY (teacher-facing naming):
The atomic teaching chunk is called a "unit" in ALL teacher-facing prose — teacher_notes, activity titles, homework. The token "period" is retained ONLY in (a) schema field names (period_number, period_duration_minutes, periods[], etc.) and (b) the scheduling/allocation budget (period schedule, period count, per-period budget). Never write "period" in prose the teacher reads; "session" is outside the register too.

THE SELF-CONTAINED REGISTER (binds Rules 7 and 10)
Three things no time band or teacher note may do, each because the platform enforces it:
1. NAME A CLOCK QUANTITY — the platform scales every band's minutes in proportion to the sitting that carries it, so a stated number is falsified silently: no "for three minutes", "the remaining time", "half the session". Where a task is genuinely brief or genuinely long, say so in kind — "a quick individual calculation", "an extended investigation" — never in number.
2. POINT FORWARD OR CLAIM COMPLETION — a teacher's plan may end, or hand over to a companion variant's unit, after any unit, so "the next unit", "as we will see", "having covered all three models" are wrong for someone. Each unit closes on its own ground.
3. NAME CALENDAR TIME — Aruvi keeps no calendar and sittings do not map to days: today, yesterday, this week, next class are unknowable at authoring.
Backward continuity is welcome, and is best carried by naming the content built on ("Having established that mass and charge are carried by different particles, …" — Rule 10's continuity link) rather than a unit's position.
